title: Commands
description: Tell someone what to do or not to do, with or without pronouns.

guide.summary: Commands tell someone to do something, or not to do it. French has only three command forms — tu, nous and vous — and the whole topic is knowing which form to write, what happens to the final s, and where the pronouns go.

sections.title: Which command form: tu, nous or vous?
sections.text: A command has no subject pronoun: the verb stands alone. Only three persons exist, so first decide who you are speaking to.

rows: one friend, child or family member
gives an order or makes a request
several people, or one person you address politely
gives an order or makes a request

steps: Ask who the order is aimed at: one friend, one stranger, or several people.
One friend or child: tu. Several people or a polite single person: vous.
If English says “let’s …”, use the nous form.

examples.fr: Parle plus lentement, s’il te plaît.

watch: The nous form is a suggestion, not an order: allons-y means “let’s go”.
Never keep the subject: write the verb alone, not “tu ferme”.
Clues in the sentence tell you the person: s’il te plaît and ton frère mean tu; les enfants and vos devoirs mean vous.

sections.title: Build the form from the present
sections.text: For almost every verb the command is simply the present form with the subject pronoun deleted. Nothing else changes, irregular verbs included.
steps: Conjugate the verb in the present for tu, nous or vous.
Delete the subject pronoun and keep the verb letter for letter.
Only -er verbs and aller change further: see the next section.
watch: A verb irregular in the present stays irregular here: vous faites, vous dites.
Finir-type verbs keep -iss- in the plural: nous finissons, vous finissez.
An infinitive (finir, venir) and a past participle (venu, fermé) never give an order.

sections.title: Why an -er verb has no s in the tu command
sections.text: In the tu command, -er verbs and aller drop the final s of the present. Verbs like ouvrir and offrir, whose tu form also ends in -es, drop it too.
steps: Write the tu form of the present.
If the verb is an -er verb, aller, or an ouvrir-type verb, cut the final s.
Every other verb keeps its s: prends, finis, attends.

examples.fr: Ferme la porte, s’il te plaît.

watch: The nous and vous forms lose nothing: parlons, parlez, mangeons.
Manger keeps its e before -ons: mangeons, not “mangons”.
Mange (an order) and mangé (a past participle) are different words.

sections.title: The s comes back before y and en
sections.text: When y or en follows the tu command straight away, the dropped s returns so the two words link in speech. The pronoun is attached with a hyphen.
steps: Build the tu command as usual, without its s.
Look at the word right after the verb: if it is y or en, put the s back.
Join the verb and the pronoun with a hyphen.

examples.en: There is cake left: have some!

watch: The s returns only before y and en, never before other words: va à la gare.
The hyphen is compulsory: vas-y, not “vas y”.
This only concerns the tu form; allez-y and allons-y never change.

sections.title: Être, avoir and savoir: learn the nine forms
sections.text: These three verbs do not take their command from the present. Their forms have to be learnt.
steps: Spot the verb: être, avoir or savoir.
Read the person from the sentence, then take that column of the table.
Place ne … pas around the form as with any other verb.
watch: Es, avez and sais are present forms: they give no order.
The tu form of être ends in s, but the tu forms of avoir and savoir do not.
Soit and soient are the forms used after que (qu’il soit là), not commands.

sections.title: Saying don’t: ne … pas around the verb
sections.text: A negative command keeps the same verb form and wraps ne … pas around it. Ne becomes n’ before a vowel.
steps: Build the command you would use in the affirmative.
Put ne (n’ before a vowel) in front of the verb and pas immediately after it.
Send any pronoun back in front of the verb, between ne and the verb.
watch: Pas comes straight after the verb, never at the end of the sentence.
Dropping ne (“mange pas !”) is spoken French; write it in full.
Ne pas + infinitive is the style of written notices (ne pas fumer), not of an order to a person.

sections.title: Reflexive commands: where does the pronoun go?
sections.text: A reflexive verb keeps its pronoun, and the pronoun moves with the negation: behind the verb when the command is affirmative, in front of it when it is negative. Behind the verb, te becomes toi.
steps: Choose the person: tu, nous or vous, and take the matching pronoun.
Affirmative: verb first, then the pronoun, joined by a hyphen (te becomes toi).
Negative: ne, then the pronoun, then the verb, then pas.
watch: The pronoun must match the verb: no “levez-toi”, no “dépêchons-vous”.
Never write “-te” after the verb; the stressed form is toi.
The hyphen belongs to the affirmative only: in the negative the pronoun is a separate word.

sections.title: Object pronouns with a command
sections.text: Object pronouns follow the same rule as reflexive ones: behind the verb with a hyphen in the affirmative, in front of the verb in the negative. Me and te become moi and toi behind the verb, and with two pronouns le, la or les comes first.
steps: Choose the pronoun that replaces the noun, matching its gender and number.
Affirmative: attach it behind the verb with a hyphen; me becomes moi and te becomes toi.
Negative: put it back between ne and the verb, with pas after the verb.
With two pronouns behind the verb, le, la or les comes before moi, toi, lui or leur.
watch: Never “-me” or “-te” behind the verb.
Le and la become l’ before a vowel: ne l’écoute pas.
Lui and leur replace a person after à (parle-lui); a direct object takes le, la or les.

steps: Write the tu form of the present first.
If the verb ends in -er, or is aller or an ouvrir-type verb, cut the final s.
For nous and vous, take the present form unchanged and drop the subject.
Read the person asked for: tu, nous or vous.
Conjugate the verb in the present for that person.
Delete the subject pronoun and change nothing else; only -er verbs and aller lose a letter.
Build the tu command as usual, without its s.
Check the word right after the verb: if it is y or en, put the s back.
Join the verb and the pronoun with a hyphen.
Ask whether the verb is être, avoir or savoir: their commands are not the present forms.
Find the person from the clues in the sentence.
Take that form from the table and leave it unchanged inside ne … pas.
Build the command form you would use in the affirmative.
Put ne (n’ before a vowel) before the verb and pas straight after it.
Move any pronoun in front of the verb, between ne and the verb.
Match the pronoun to the person of the verb: with tu, with nous, with vous.
Affirmative: pronoun behind the verb, hyphen, stressed form.
Negative: pronoun in front of the verb, between ne and the verb.
Decide which pronoun replaces the noun, matching gender and number.
Affirmative: behind the verb with a hyphen, me and te in their stressed forms.
Negative: in front of the verb, between ne and the verb, with pas after the verb.

exercises.feedback: In a negative command, the pronoun comes before the verb.
exercises.explanation: In the negative, the pronoun stays in front: ne te couche pas.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is still attached behind the verb, as in an affirmative order. A negative command puts it back in front.

answers: Ne toi couche pas trop tard.
mistakes.why: The pronoun is in the right place now, but toi is the stressed form used only behind an affirmative command.

answers: Ne te couches pas trop tard.
mistakes.why: Coucher is an -er verb; its tu command has no final s.

alternatives.message: In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun is joined to the verb with a hyphen.

exercises.hint: Use the nous command and put the pronoun after the verb.
exercises.feedback: The reflexive pronoun follows the nous command with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous dépêchons becomes dépêchons-nous.

mistakes.why: That is a statement: “we are hurrying”. A command drops the subject and moves the pronoun behind the verb.
That orders other people to hurry; “let’s” includes yourself.
The pronoun does not match the verb: a nous form carries the nous pronoun.
That is the dictionary form of the verb with its pronoun, not an order.

exercises.instruction: Write se laver as a vous command, with its pronoun.
exercises.source: Les enfants, ____ les mains avant le dîner !

alternatives.message: In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun is joined to the verb with a hyphen.
In an affirmative command, the pronoun goes after the verb: lavez-vous.

exercises.hint: The pronoun goes after the verb in an affirmative command.
exercises.feedback: Put vous after the verb, joined with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Vous vous lavez becomes lavez-vous.

mistakes.why: That is the present statement: it says what the children do, instead of telling them to do it.
Toi belongs with a tu command, but the verb here is aimed at several children.
That speaks to one child; les enfants means you are addressing several.
Laver is the infinitive; the blank needs the command form with its pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Replace le livre with a pronoun.

alternatives.message: In an affirmative command, the pronoun goes after the verb: prends-le.
In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun is joined to the verb with a hyphen.

exercises.hint: In an affirmative command, the pronoun goes after the verb.
exercises.feedback: Put the pronoun after the verb with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Le livre becomes le, placed after the verb: prends-le.

mistakes.why: Le livre is still written out; the task is to put in its place the pronoun that stands for it.
La stands for a feminine noun, and livre is masculine.
Lui replaces a person after à (parle-lui). A book that is taken directly needs a direct-object pronoun.
The pronoun and the noun name the same thing, so keeping both says it twice.

exercises.hint: In the negative, the pronoun moves back in front of the verb.
exercises.feedback: In a negative command, the pronoun comes before the verb, inside ne…pas.
exercises.explanation: Regarde-les becomes ne les regarde pas.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has stayed behind the verb as in the affirmative order; a negative command sends it back in front of the verb.
Regarder is an -er verb: its tu command drops the final s of tu regardes.
An object pronoun never stands alone after pas; it always leans on the verb.
Ne has been dropped, which belongs to casual speech, and the pronoun is still in its affirmative place.

exercises.hint: After the verb, me changes form. Donner is an -er verb.
exercises.feedback: Check the pronoun’s position and form, and the -er ending.
exercises.explanation: Donne-moi: the pronoun follows, me becomes moi, and the -er verb has no s.

mistakes.why: Me is the form used in front of the verb. Behind an affirmative command the pronoun takes its stressed form.
That is the order of a statement (tu me donnes). An affirmative command puts the pronoun behind the verb.
Donner is an -er verb, so its tu command has no final s; the s returns only before y or en.

exercises.hint: This command is negative. Where does the pronoun go?
exercises.feedback: In a negative command, the pronoun comes before the verb, after ne.
exercises.explanation: In the negative, the pronoun stays in front: ne le mange pas.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is in its affirmative place, behind the verb. A negative command puts it back in front of the verb.
The pronoun has jumped in front of ne. Ne always opens the negation, and the pronoun sits between it and the verb.
An object pronoun never follows pas, and the hyphen belongs to affirmative commands only.

exercises.instruction: Write the tu command of appeler followed by the pronoun la.
exercises.source: Ta sœur t’attend. ____ tout de suite !

alternatives.message: In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun is joined to the verb with a hyphen.
In an affirmative command, the pronoun goes after the verb: appelle-la.

exercises.hint: The pronoun goes after the verb. Appeler doubles a letter in tu appelles.
exercises.feedback: Put la after the verb with a hyphen; the -er verb has no s.
exercises.explanation: Tu appelles becomes appelle, and la follows: appelle-la.

mistakes.why: Le stands for a masculine person or thing, and ta sœur is feminine.
Appeler is an -er verb: the tu command drops the final s of tu appelles.
Lui goes with verbs built on à (téléphone-lui). Appeler takes its object directly.
Appeler doubles its l before a silent ending, as in tu appelles; one l is not enough here.

exercises.hint: Look at the pronoun after the verb.
exercises.feedback: After the verb, me takes its stressed form.
exercises.explanation: In an affirmative command, me becomes moi: aide-moi.

mistakes.why: Me is the form used in front of the verb; behind an affirmative command the pronoun must take its stressed form.
Aider is an -er verb, so its tu command has no final s.
That is the order of a statement, and me would elide before a vowel anyway.

alternatives.message: In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun is joined to the verb with a hyphen.
In an affirmative command, the pronoun goes after the verb: regardez-les.

exercises.hint: Use the vous command, then the pronoun for them.
exercises.feedback: Put the pronoun after the verb with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Them is les, placed after the verb: regardez-les.

mistakes.why: That speaks to one person, and the instruction says several.
Leur replaces people after à (parle-leur). Regarder looks at them directly, so it takes a direct-object pronoun.
French regarder needs no preposition: what you look at is a direct object, with no à.
Eux is the stressed pronoun used after prepositions (avec eux), not the object of a verb.
